source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: Reviews 12 theories of syllogistic inference in three families: heuristic, formal-rule, and model/diagram-based. Tests 7 of them against 6 data sets of all 64 premise pairs. None fits well. Model-based theories beat heuristic ones on average.
numbers: 6 experiments, N = 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 56 (Johnson-Laird and Steedman 1978 twice; Johnson-Laird and Bara 1984; Bara et al. 1995 teens and adults; Roberts et al. 2001). Aggregate correct predictions: model-based 76%, heuristic 66%.
quote: None of the 12 theories provides an adequate account
limits: Only 7 of 12 theories had usable predictions. Data come mostly from two labs and use students. Johnson-Laird is a proponent of one of the theories compared.
agent_relevance: Gives the ground-truth difficulty map of the 64 syllogisms (use as the human baseline and as a test set for S4). No single mechanism explains human errors, so do not hard-code one human-error model into the agent.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis (reliability of the data)
finding: Across the 6 studies the difficulty order of syllogisms is very stable, so syllogism difficulty is a property of the problem, not of the lab. Hard problems also give more varied wrong answers.
numbers: Kendall W = .86 for 27 valid syllogisms; W = .64 for 37 problems with no valid conclusion; W = .45 for response entropy; entropy vs accuracy r = -0.52. A response counted as reliable if given on at least 16% of trials (chance 1/9). Easiest valid problem 90% correct, hardest 1%.
quote: studies of syllogistic reasoning in the psychological laboratory yield highly correlated results
limits: Response coding treats 9 possible responses (4 moods x 2 term orders, plus nothing follows). Noise threshold of 16% is a choice.
agent_relevance: Per-problem difficulty and answer entropy can drive S0 gate and S2 budget: spend more checking effort where human (and likely model) answers are spread out.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis (Table 8 results)
finding: Each theory trades hits against false alarms. Mental models predicts almost every observed answer but also predicts many nobody gives. Illicit conversion predicts too few answers. Verbal models gave the best balance but is unstable across data sets.
numbers: Hits: mental models 95%, verbal models 63%, matching 59%, PHM 52%, atmosphere 51%, PSYCOP 44%, conversion 44%. Correct rejections: conversion 93%, verbal models 90%, atmosphere 85%, PSYCOP 85%, PHM 79%, mental models 74%, matching 74%. Overall correct: verbal models 84%, conversion 83%, mental models 78%, atmosphere 78%, PSYCOP 77%, PHM 73%, matching 71%. Verbal models heterogeneity I2 = 52%, Q = 10.69, p = .06. Mental models hits show publication-bias signal (z = 2.03, p < .05).
limits: Precision/recall style scoring against a 16% threshold; verbal-model predictions come from default parameters only.
agent_relevance: A model that outputs many plausible conclusions (high recall) needs a code-side filter for precision. This matches our rule that code selects (G5).

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) (phenomena section: figural effect)
finding: Term order in the premises (the figure) biases which way the conclusion is written. Figure 1 (A-B, B-C) gives A-C conclusions; figure 2 gives C-A. When the only valid conclusion runs against the bias, accuracy collapses.
numbers: Johnson-Laird and Steedman 1978 example: 15 of 17 wrote 'Some A are C' for Some A are B, All B are C; 16 of 17 wrote 'Some C are A' for the reversed order. Valid conclusion that fits the bias about 80% correct, violating it about 20%. Nothing-follows correct by figure (Johnson-Laird and Bara 1984, 10 s limit): Fig 1 50%, Fig 2 57%, Fig 3 70%, Fig 4 86% (Jonckheere z = 3.32, p < .001).
limits: Authors favour Oberauer's semantic account over working-memory 'first in, first out'. Competing explanations remain.
agent_relevance: Order of terms in a prompt can steer a language model the same way. Normalise premise order in S1 and test both orders; disagreement across orders is a signal for G1.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) (heuristic theories section: atmosphere, matching, conversion)
finding: Atmosphere (Woodworth and Sells 1935; Begg and Denny 1969 rule): any negative premise gives a negative conclusion; any 'some' premise gives a 'some' conclusion; else universal affirmative. It cannot explain correct 'nothing follows' answers, since some conclusion always fits. Matching (Wetherick and Gilhooly 1995): choose the conclusion mood of the most conservative premise, rank E, O, I, A. Illicit conversion (Chapman and Chapman 1959): All A are B read as All B are A.
numbers: 'Only' premises: when both premises used 'only', 16% of conclusions contained it; with one 'only' premise, 2%. Atmosphere fails here.
quote: there is always a conclusion that fits the atmosphere of the premises
limits: Atmosphere overlaps with valid inference because most valid conclusions fit it. Only invalid problems separate theories.
agent_relevance: Atmosphere is a cheap detector of shallow pattern answers. Our checker can flag any model answer that equals the atmosphere prediction on an invalid-by-construction item.

source: Chater and Oaksford (1999) The probability heuristics model of syllogistic reasoning
finding: PHM treats quantifiers as probability statements ranked by informativeness (all > most > few > some > none > some-not). People use fast heuristics: min-heuristic (conclusion has the quantifier of the least informative premise), p-entailment (next-best is a weaker implied form), attachment (subject of the conclusion comes from the min-premise end term), and max-heuristic (confidence grows with the informativeness of the most informative premise). The heuristics usually find the probabilistically valid (p-valid) conclusion.
numbers: Min-heuristic matches the p-valid conclusion type in 22 of 31 p-valid classical syllogisms; with most and few added, 32 of 38 p-valid. 31 orthodox pairs are p-valid vs 27 logically valid.
quote: choose the type of the least informative premise as the type of the conclusion
limits: Assumes people cannot test conclusions for validity. Cannot explain why some people are far more accurate (Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2012 critique).
agent_relevance: The min-heuristic is a compact, checkable rule: use it as a code-side baseline predictor and as a trap detector. A model answer that follows min but is logically invalid is the typical human-like error.

source: Chater and Oaksford (1999) PHM meta-analysis of five data sets
finding: PHM with 6 fitted parameters accounts for syllogism responses over all 64 problems. The min-heuristic explains nearly all wrong conclusions on invalid problems, so the same strategy covers valid and invalid items. Logic adds only a small extra effect.
numbers: Data: Dickstein 1978 (N = 22 and 76), Johnson-Laird and Steedman 1978 (N = 20, 20), Johnson-Laird and Bara 1984 (N = 20). 320 data points: r(318) = .90, RMS .30, over 80% of variance. Min-heuristic accounts for 95.17% of non-NVC conclusions on invalid syllogisms. Logically correct on only 51.8% of trials: 64.9% valid, 46.8% invalid. Fitted max-premise parameters for conclusion order: pA 55.30, pI 24.08, pE 15.97, pO 15.00.
limits: 6 parameters fitted to 320 points. Different task formats (forced choice vs production) pooled. Fit tells fit, not mechanism.
agent_relevance: Shows that most human syllogism errors are an informational strategy, not noise. A language model can share it. Useful as an error taxonomy for the S4 test items.

source: Chater and Oaksford (1999) PHM vs mental models (attachment and figure)
finding: Attachment explains the figural effect and goes beyond it: conclusion type, not just figure, sets term order. Mental models predicts the figure difficulty order 4 > 1 > 2 > 3, which the meta-analysis does not confirm. Attachment fails on the 8 same-type syllogisms in figures 2 and 3, which is where people say nothing follows.
numbers: For all 32 syllogisms in figures 1 and 4 attachment agrees with the figural effect. Of 24 in figures 2 and 3 where attachment makes a prediction, 22 conformed, 1 violated, 1 tie. 16 'doubles' (both premises same type) vs 48 singles used to test NVC rate.
limits: 20 syllogisms have no attachment prediction; people then prefer A-C order. EO syllogisms sometimes get E conclusions that PHM does not predict.
agent_relevance: Predicts when a model will refuse to answer: symmetric same-type premises. Our agent should treat 'nothing follows' there as a hypothesis to test, not a default.

source: Oaksford, Roberts and Chater (2002) Relative informativeness of quantifiers used in syllogistic reasoning
finding: Follow-up to resolve an anomaly in PHM: 'few' did not behave as more informative than 'some' in Chater and Oaksford's own experiments. Three experiments had people rank quantifiers for fit to a stated proportion. Splitting positive quantifiers (all, most, some) from negative ones (few, none, some-not) fixes the ordering.
numbers: Experiment 1 N = 81 (verbal and visual groups), Experiment 2 N = 40 (rank all six quantifiers; Kendall W mean .84, SD .04), Experiment 3 N = 50 (one quantifier per trial, no response competition). No difference in informativeness between 'few' and 'some' except in Experiment 2.
limits: Rescues the model after the fact. The 'few' vs 'some' result depended on the task format.
agent_relevance: Quantifier meaning is graded and context dependent. When an item uses most/few/some, S1 should restate the quantifier as a numeric range before reasoning.

source: Oaksford, Chater and Larkin (2000) Probabilities and polarity biases in conditional inference
finding: Conditional inference (MP, DA, AC, MT) is modelled as conditional probability. The rule 'if p then q' is a 2x2 table with parameters a = P(p), b = P(q) and exceptions e = P(not-q given p). The chance of drawing each inference is a conditional probability. Negative-conclusion bias is then a high-probability conclusion effect, because negated categories are large.
numbers: Model: MP = P(q|p) = 1 - e; MT, DA and AC follow from a, b and e. With exceptions, DA, AC and MT endorsement should rise with the probability of the conclusion.
quote: negations define higher probability categories than their affirmative counterparts
limits: Needs parameters a, b, e per rule, three data points per rule in the fits. Authors admit the model is not a full theory of negation.
agent_relevance: Gives a calculable target: acceptability of a conditional inference should follow P(conclusion|premise). The agent can compute it from stated frequencies instead of guessing.

source: Oaksford, Chater and Larkin (2000) Experiment 1
finding: Manipulating the probability of antecedent and consequent (machine quality-control cards) produced a high-probability conclusion effect for DA, AC and MT, close to significant for MP. The converse inferences ranked DA' > AC' > MT' > MP', the reverse of what logic or the standard order predicts.
numbers: N = 30 Warwick undergraduates, 4 x 2 x 2 x 2 within design, 7-point acceptance ratings. Overall high vs low conclusion F(1,87) = 22.90, p < .0001 (M 2.93 vs 2.33). MT: M 5.98 vs 5.45, F = 5.78, p < .025. MP: 6.62 vs 6.20, F = 3.53, p = .064. Converse: DA' 3.85 vs 3.10, AC' 3.40 vs 2.43. Model fit R2 on individual data reported good.
limits: Used 'all' rule form and a prediction framing, so probability was cued. No low-probability premise effect; the HL rule seems to have been reinterpreted.
agent_relevance: People (and likely models) accept more inferences when the conclusion is a common category. A fixed prompt that mixes base rates will shift answers; hold them constant when testing.

source: Oaksford, Chater and Larkin (2000) Experiments 2 and 3
finding: Exp 2 used standard 'if then' and removed exceptions; MT then rose toward MP, and implicit negations (binary materials) removed the extra MT difficulty but not DA. Exp 3 used pretested everyday contents with no probability cues; effects were weaker but present. Low-probability premise effects were unreliable or artifacts.
numbers: Exp 2 N = 25: high vs low conclusion F(1,72) = 28.91, p < .0001 (M 2.60 vs 1.68); AC low-premise effect F(1,72) = 6.84, p < .025; model mean R2 = .93, split-half R2 = .96. Exp 3 N = 20, 481 predicates, 91 rules, 8 chosen: AC high vs low F(1,57) = 4.62; MT F(1,57) = 4.54; DA n.s. (p = .26); mean R2 = .92; split-half R2 = .84.
limits: Small samples (20 to 30). Model has free parameters per participant. Schroyens and Schaeken (2003) found the deductive and probabilistic accounts not isomorphic; authors replied in 2003.
agent_relevance: The negation effect is not only a language quirk. Reframe negated premises into positive contrast sets in S1 only if a test shows it helps.

source: Byrne (1989) Suppressing valid inferences with conditionals (figures as quoted in secondary sources)
finding: Adding a second conditional about an additional requirement (library must be open) cuts modus ponens sharply. Adding one with an alternative antecedent (textbook to read) leaves MP intact but cuts AC and DA. Suppression of valid MP and MT is the key challenge for formal-rule theories.
numbers: MP: 96% simple, 96% alternative, 38% additional. AC: 71% simple falling to 13% with alternative. MT with additional antecedent: 33%. (Table in the secondary source was garbled for MT, DA and some cells, so only these cells are cited.)
limits: Original paper not obtained; the numbers come from an arXiv paper and a lecture slide deck that quote Byrne's table. A search snippet gave 16% instead of 13% for AC-alternative, so check. College students, written materials.
agent_relevance: A single extra premise can make a model withhold a valid inference. Test items should include a distractor conditional and check that the answer does not flip (G3 mutated input).

source: Dietz and Holldobler (2016) Byrne's suppression task (lecture slides)
finding: Shows the three argument types and the answer pattern: the majority conclude 'she will stay late' with the simple or alternative premise, but the majority choose 'I don't know' with the additional-antecedent premise, though MP is classically valid. Treats the task via logic programs with abnormality atoms (Stenning and van Lambalgen 2008) under weak completion semantics.
numbers: Byrne row quoted: 96%, 96%, 38% for MP over simple, alternative, additional.
limits: Teaching slides, not primary data. Weak completion semantics models the pattern; it does not prove people use it.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal-solver recipe: encode a rule with a default 'no abnormality' condition; extra premises add abnormality conditions. This is the logic of defeasible rules, usable in a code checker.

source: Human Conditional Reasoning in Answer Set Programming (arXiv 2311.04412), review of the Stenning and van Lambalgen line
finding: Answer-set-programming account of conditional reasoning handles suppression (nonmonotonic reasoning) and Wason selection by treating AC and DA as completion inferences. It characterises suppression of DA and AC but, as the authors note, does not capture suppression of valid AA (MP) under additional antecedents with the completion method alone.
numbers: Reports Byrne's 1989 table (MP 96, 96, 38).
limits: A theory paper with worked programs, no new human data. Admits one failed case (additional-antecedent MP).
agent_relevance: Shows a formal solver for conditionals needs defaults and exceptions, not plain material implication. A checker that treats 'if' as strict logic will disagree with humans and with good models on exception-laden items.

source: Neth and Beller (1999) How knowledge interferes with reasoning: suppression effects by content and context
finding: Extends suppression beyond Byrne's one scenario to 15 scenarios with measured sufficiency and necessity. Both content and context matter: perceived necessary-but-insufficient conditions raise AC and DA; an extra alternative-antecedent conditional cuts AC and DA to about 15%; an additive conditional cuts MP and MT.
numbers: Exp 2 N = 50 Freiburg volunteers. Rates by context (out of 150): only p/q MP 92.7, MT 75.3, AC 58.0, DA 62.0; plus alternative 92.7, 78.0, 16.0, 14.0; plus additive 64.0, 46.7, 50.0, 47.3. MP and MT with sufficient condition 91.7% vs 81.7% reference (chi2 = 4.01, p < .05). AC and DA with necessary condition 92.5% vs 40.0% (chi2 = 68.91, p < .01). Insufficient condition did not reduce MP and MT (77.5% vs 81.7%, n.s.).
limits: Only the 'raise' predictions held; 'lower' predictions (insufficient, unnecessary) did not. Between-context comparison partly within, partly across item sets. Conference paper, one lab.
agent_relevance: Background knowledge of necessity and sufficiency changes the inference more than form does. The agent should extract what the facts say about necessary vs sufficient (S1) before applying an inference rule.

source: Neth and Beller (1999) Experiment 3
finding: When people choose the proper wording for a relation between p and q, they pick the formally right direction even when their syllogism answers deviated. So many so-called errors reflect reinterpretation of the premise, not failure to apply logic.
numbers: Overall 68.2% of choices matched the formally appropriate wording; 79.2% in context 'only p/q', 64.0% with alternative, 61.3% with additive. 28 of 30 participants chose the appropriate converse form in one scenario test.
limits: Multiple-choice format; N about 30. Reinterpretation claim is inferred, not observed directly.
agent_relevance: Supports a restate-the-rule step (S1): make the model write the rule in both directions and say which one the text supports, before drawing any inference.

source: Girotto and Johnson-Laird (2004) The probability of conditionals
finding: Tests the 'new paradigm' claim that the probability of 'if A then C' equals the conditional probability P(C|A). Mental model theory predicts a gap because conditionals are represented by few explicit models. Naive people judged conditional probabilities well but probabilities of the conditional poorly, usually underestimating the complete value.
numbers: Exp 1 N = 48 (card problems): conditional probability correct 68% vs complete probability of the conditional 17% (Wilcoxon z = 11.8, p < .00005); 0%, 8%, 42% complete across problems 1 to 3; 45 of 48 underestimated more than overestimated. Exp 2 N = 20: 87% vs 32%; 10%, 55%, 100% complete over problems 2, 3, 4 (18 of 20 in trend direction).
limits: Authors are the model theory camp. Four participants in Exp 1 converted the question to P(C|A) anyway. Exp 1 think-aloud replication N = 10 removed some unexpected responses.
agent_relevance: The probability of 'if A then C' and P(C|A) are different questions. For a probability-of-conditional item, the prompt should say which one is asked, and code should compute from the explicit possibilities.

source: Girotto and Johnson-Laird (2004), review of rival evidence (Evans, Handley and Over 2003; Oberauer and Wilhelm 2003)
finding: Evidence for the conditional-probability hypothesis is mixed. Evans et al. (2003): fewer counterexample cards gave a higher rated probability. Oberauer and Wilhelm (2003): only some people gave equal values for P(q|p) and P(if p then q).
numbers: Evans et al. (as quoted): pack of 30 cards, 6 yellow circles; with 2 yellow diamonds mean rating 54%, with 12 yellow diamonds 37%. Oberauer and Wilhelm (as quoted): 52% gave the same value in Experiment 1B; 23% did consistently in Experiment 1A.
limits: Second-hand figures quoted inside a rival camp's paper. The search summary of Evans et al. says half used conditional probability and most others the conjunction P(pq); that summary was not opened in full text.
agent_relevance: Human 'probability of if' judgments are split between P(q|p), the conjunction and others. A scaffold must define the target quantity; it cannot rely on a shared intuition.

source: van Rooij and Schulz (2019) Conditionals, causality and conditional probability
finding: Acceptability of an indicative conditional tracks conditional probability but needs more: a dependence between antecedent and consequent. They propose one causal dependence condition (relative difference) that reduces to conditional probability under natural circumstances.
numbers: Relative difference compares P(e|i) with P(e|not-i); the required gap shrinks as P(e|i) rises. Cites Douven (2008, 2016), Skovgaard-Olsen et al. (2016, 2017), Douven and Verbrugge (2010).
limits: A theory paper; does not run new experiments. Restricted to conditionals that accept 'then'. Skovgaard-Olsen and colleagues argue the dependence requirement is pragmatic rather than semantic.
agent_relevance: A conditional with high P(q|p) but no link between p and q reads as odd to people. The agent should flag irrelevant conditionals (relevance effect) instead of accepting them as premises.

source: Khemlani (2020) Psychological theories of syllogistic reasoning (chapter)
finding: After the meta-analysis, two integrated theories mix heuristic and deliberate steps: Hattori's probabilistic sampling model and mReasoner (a stochastic mental-model program). mReasoner builds an initial model from the premises, then optionally searches for counterexamples. It handles any number of premises.
numbers: mReasoner fit to the meta-analysis data r = 0.82 (as shown on the chapter figure). Von Stoerring ran the first reasoning experiments in 1908.
limits: Authored by a mReasoner developer. Figure text was only partly legible in extraction. mReasoner cannot yet explain belief bias; a prototype is described only.
agent_relevance: Suggests a two-pass design: one fast guess, then a counterexample search triggered by a signal (G1). The counterexample search is the part code can check.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) (individual differences and strategies)
finding: People differ a lot in accuracy and strategy. Some never look for alternative models and rarely say nothing follows. Others search but cannot state a conclusion common to all models, and say nothing follows too often. Working-memory capacity correlates with accuracy.
numbers: Accuracy across participants from 15% to 85% correct valid conclusions. Mean valid conclusions 55% at a selective US university (Johnson-Laird and Steedman) vs 37% at a non-selective Italian university (Johnson-Laird and Bara 1984). Unpublished working-memory correlation about .7 (with Oakhill). Strategy use: some build model sequences on 75% of problems, one participant on 8%.
limits: The .7 correlation is unpublished, reported second-hand. Strategy classifications come from think-aloud and drawing studies with small N.
agent_relevance: Expect the same split in sampled attempts: some do not search for counterexamples at all. A code-counted check for 'did the attempt state a counterexample' is cheaper than judging text.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) (existential import and conversion)
finding: Whether 'All A are B' implies that A exist changes which syllogisms are valid. The classical (Aristotelian) logic count of valid problems is 27 only if the implicature is allowed; PSYCOP needs the implicature to reach the 27. Definite article wording ('all the artists') cues existence. Conversion errors from All A are B to All B are A have a probabilistic basis.
numbers: 27 valid and 37 invalid problems among the 64. PSYCOP with Gricean implicatures yields the 27.
limits: Whether participants assume existence depends on wording and instructions; the meta-analysis pools studies with different wording.
agent_relevance: Our benchmark items must state whether sets are non-empty. A scaffold should ask this in S1 or the same item can score differently under two conventions.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) (PSYCOP and verbal models)
finding: Formal-rule accounts: Rips's PSYCOP uses natural-deduction rules plus implicatures; Polk and Newell's verbal reasoning model uses linguistic encoding and re-encoding without counterexample search. Both explain errors by failures of encoding or search, not by wrong rules.
numbers: PSYCOP hits 44%, correct rejections 85%, overall 77%. Verbal models overall 84%, marginal heterogeneity (I2 = 52%).
limits: Polk-Newell predictions use default parameters; others could improve the fit. Rules-based accounts struggle to predict erroneous inferences without added assumptions.
agent_relevance: Rule-based solvers give a clean code check for validity (derive or fail), at the cost of not predicting the typical wrong answers.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) (content and belief effects, noted)
finding: Believable conclusions are accepted more often than unbelievable ones, and the effect is larger for invalid conclusions. Details are in the earlier belief-bias document in this series.
numbers: Not re-derived here.
limits: Brief summary; see the belief bias file.
agent_relevance: Overlaps with the belief-bias subfield. Keep one test pair set there, not a second one here.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt and Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of large language models as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: Zero-shot chain-of-thought LLaMA and Pythia models on all 64 schemas with pseudo-words and real words. Models avoid saying nothing follows. Their wrong answers on invalid items follow atmosphere. In-context examples raise valid accuracy but not invalid accuracy and make answers more contradictory. Fine-tuning on form removes most content effects.
numbers: Human accuracy used as reference: 44.63% valid, 40.97% invalid (Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2012). LLaMA-3 70B instruct: 58.89% on valid, 32.50% on invalid. Atmosphere predicts 92% of LLaMA zero-shot-CoT correct valid conclusions and 82.97% of its invalid-schema errors, 62.79% of valid-schema errors. Atmosphere predicts 62.50% of correct valid conclusions overall and 0% on invalid.
limits: Open models only (Pythia, LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3 sizes up to 70B). Fine-tuned models trained on the same 64 schemas can leak. Answers annotated with LLaMA-3 8B (93.42% agreement with human on 441 conclusions).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a plain LLM is an atmosphere reasoner on syllogisms and rarely says 'no valid conclusion'. For our scaffold, the invalid half of the items is where a checker adds value (counterexample search in code).

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt and Bernardi (2024), consistency and multi-premise results
finding: Models produce contradictory conclusion pairs (for example 'All a are b' with 'Some a are not b') more often after in-context learning. Supervised fine-tuned LLaMA produced almost no contradictions (0.31%). Accuracy drops when the number of premises goes beyond what was seen.
numbers: 28 schemas with an A premise used for the multi-premise test. LLaMA completeness: 43.14% in zero-shot vs 96.93% (ICL variants 72.93% and 76.24%).
limits: Consistency measured only on the believable subset. Fine-tuned Pythia became less consistent when accuracy rose.
agent_relevance: A cheap code check: reject any answer set containing a contradictory pair (A with O, E with I). It needs no model.

source: Oaksford, Chater and Larkin (2000), meta-analysis of the negations paradigm
finding: Reports the earlier negations-paradigm findings (Evans 1977; Pollard and Evans 1980; Wildman and Fletcher 1977; Evans et al. 1995): negative conclusion bias is strongest for DA and MT. Evans et al. read this as a double-negation effect. Evans and Handley (1999) found affirmative-premise bias with implicit negations but not negative conclusion bias.
numbers: Specific effect sizes of the earlier studies were not extracted this session.
limits: Second-hand description of the older studies inside a paper by competing theorists. Different accounts (double negation, affirmative premise bias, high-probability conclusion) predict different patterns.
agent_relevance: Negations are a known trap for MT and DA. Add negated-consequent items to the S4 test set and check the answer on both the explicit and implicit forms.

source: Oaksford, Chater and Larkin (2000), the model's key predictions
finding: Three predictions: a high-probability conclusion effect for DA, AC and MT; a low-probability premise effect for AC (and DA when the conclusion probability exceeds the exceptions parameter); opposite effects for the converse inferences. Without exceptions MT should be drawn regardless of probabilities.
numbers: Converse order observed in Exp 1 and Exp 2: DA' > AC' > MT' > MP'.
limits: Only the first and third predictions held consistently; the low-probability premise effect was weak or artifactual (Exp 2 and 3).
agent_relevance: The model gives falsifiable direction predictions for probe items, so we can check whether an LLM follows human base-rate patterns or logic.
